title: Psalm 69:1–36
context: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. Of David. Waters to the neck, zeal for the house, gall and sour wine, imprecations on persecutors, then praise that pleases more than sacrifice and a promise that God will save Zion.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on drowning distress, zeal for God’s house, vinegar at the cross, and serious imprecation, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Zeal—That fervent love which I have for thy house and service, and glory, and people. Eaten—Exhausted my spirits. Upon me—I have been as deeply affected with thy reproaches, as with mine own. This tho' truly belonging to David, yet was also directed by the spirit of God in him, to represent the disposition and condition of Christ, in whom it was more fully accomplished, to whom therefore it is applied in the New Testament, the first part of it, John 2:17, and the latter, Rom 15:3. Vinegar—These things were metaphorically fulfilled in David, but properly in Christ.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Ps 69:9, 21)

reformed.quote: For the zeal of thy house hath eaten me up… David… affirms that he is fighting in God’s quarrel… by the zeal for the Church of God with which his soul was inflamed… It is, therefore, not surprising to find the Evangelists applying this passage to Christ (John 2:17). In like manner, Paul, in Romans 15:3… They put gall into my meat… the Apostle John justly declares that this Scripture was fulfilled when the soldiers gave Christ vinegar to drink upon the cross (John 19:28–30).

verses.text: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck!
verses.arminianNotes:
Waters to the neck—save me. Wesley: waters mean tribulations. The cry is desperate and authentic.

Drowning distress does not nullify prayer; grace enables the call when the soul is nearly under.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: waters enter unto the heart—suffocation forced them in. Even a courageous man reaches the brink of despair. Both hear: save me is the first word.

verses.text: I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deep mire, no foothold; flood sweeps. Standing is gone.

Both camps hear utter helplessness—deliverance must come from outside the slough.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: in mire there is no springing up; flood brings disorder. No foothold left.

verses.text: I am weary with my crying. My throat is dry. My eyes fail looking for my God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Weary crying; throat parched; eyes dim waiting.

Waiting is persevering faith that can still grow faint—keep crying.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: weary does not mean he quit; hoarse throat and failing eyes mark untiring perseverance. Both see: waiting for God.

verses.text: Those who hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of my head. Those who want to cut me off, being my enemies wrongfully, are mighty. I have to restore what I didn’t take away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hate without cause; restore what I did not steal. Wesley: restored for peace’s sake. John 15:25 cites without-cause hatred of Christ.

Innocent suffering under lies is deeply felt.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: mortal hatred kingdom-wide; without cause; liars. Good conscience under false accusation. Shared christology: hated without cause.

verses.text: God, you know my foolishness. My sins aren’t hidden from you.
verses.arminianNotes:
You know my folly; wrongs not hidden. Wesley: innocent toward enemies, yet guilty of many sins against God.

Confession before God remains necessary even when enemies lie.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: irony—he flees to God as defender of his cause; integrity known to God. Nothing hidden.
verses.keyContrast: Both place folly before God while enemies lie. Arminians typically underline sincere confession of faults toward God; Reformed readers hear ironic appeal from calumny to the God who knows.

verses.text: Don’t let those who wait for you be shamed through me, Lord GOD of Armies. Don’t let those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me, God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let not hopers be shamed through me. Wesley: if they see me forsaken they will be discouraged.

One believer’s fall can stumble seekers.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: set forth as example of hope or despair; prayer that seekers not be ashamed in him. Undisputed: corporate stake.

verses.text: Because for your sake, I have borne reproach. Shame has covered my face.
verses.arminianNotes:
For your sake—reproach and dishonor. Wesley: for obedience and zeal for glory.

Reproach for God’s sake is costly discipleship.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: cause is God’s; hatred for the anointing. For-your-sake suffering.

verses.text: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children.
verses.arminianNotes:
Stranger to brothers; alien to mother’s sons.

Both camps take the alienation seriously—loyalty to God can estrange kin.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: when devotion displeases brethren, follow God, not flesh and blood. Alien at home.

verses.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zeal for your house consumed me; reproaches of you fell on me. Wesley: applied more fully to Christ—John 2:17 and Romans 15:3.

David’s zeal prefigures Christ’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: fighting God’s quarrel; Evangelists apply to Christ; Paul applies the second member to the faithful. Shared messianic reading.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear David and, more fully, Christ. Shared christology on zeal and transferred reproach.

verses.text: When I wept and I fasted, that was to my reproach.
verses.arminianNotes:
Weeping and fasting became reproach. Wesley: wept for their impiety; they derided him.

Pious sorrow can be mocked—still do it.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: signs of pure zeal turned into mockery. No dispute here: fasting mocked.

verses.text: When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sackcloth; byword. Wesley: proverb of reproach.

Both: humiliation garb becomes joke.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: mourning tokens turned to jest. Byword.

verses.text: Those who sit in the gate talk about me. I am the song of the drunkards.
verses.arminianNotes:
Talk of the gate; drunkards’ songs. Wesley: vain idle persons in gates and markets.

Public scorn is pressure; prayer remains the answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: even judges join the mockery. Both affirm: song of drunkards.

verses.text: But as for me, my prayer is to you, LORD, in an acceptable time. God, in the abundance of your loving kindness, answer me in the truth of your salvation.
verses.arminianNotes:
Prayer at an acceptable time; steadfast love; saving faithfulness. Wesley: according to saving faithfulness.

Acceptable time is sought and waited for—pray on.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: driven from the world to God; hope shining in darkness. Where they meet: abundance of mercy.

verses.text: Deliver me out of the mire, and don’t let me sink. Let me be delivered from those who hate me, and out of the deep waters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deliver from mire, enemies, deep waters.

Both: salvation must lift out of what already swallowed.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: previously sunk; now prays not to sink—hope looking to the issue. Both traditions hear: deliver me.

verses.text: Don’t let the flood waters overwhelm me, neither let the deep swallow me up. Don’t let the pit shut its mouth on me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Flood, deep, pit’s mouth. Total engulfment feared.

Ask that the pit not close—grace hears distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: let not weight of affliction swallow. Common reading: pit language.

verses.text: Answer me, LORD, for your loving kindness is good. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, turn to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Steadfast love good; tender mercies, turn to me.

Plead mercy that can be sought.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: hard to believe God merciful when He seems angry; only His character sustains hope. Love and mercy.

verses.text: Don’t hide your face from your servant, for I am in distress. Answer me speedily!
verses.arminianNotes:
Hide not your face; distress; make haste.

Haste prayed for is sincere dependence.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: hide-face fear from delayed help; still God’s servant. Make haste.

verses.text: Draw near to my soul and redeem it. Ransom me because of my enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Draw near; redeem; ransom because of enemies.

Both: God must come close; enemies press the need.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: Draw near implies felt distance; faith still asks nearness. Both confess: redeem me.

verses.text: You know my reproach, my shame, and my dishonor. My adversaries are all before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
You know reproach, shame, dishonor; foes known.

God knows—pray from that knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: Providence not overcast; God witness of grief. All before thee.

verses.text: Reproach has broken my heart, and I am full of heaviness. I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; for comforters, but I found none.
verses.arminianNotes:
Reproach broke the heart; no pity, no comforters.

Broken heart still looks—and may find none but God.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: not without struggle; no human relief. Broken heart.

verses.text: They also gave me poison for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.
verses.arminianNotes:
Poison for food; sour wine for thirst. Wesley: metaphorically David, properly Christ.

Spirit intended Christ’s sufferings principally here.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: John rightly sees fulfillment when soldiers give vinegar. Shared messianic reading.
verses.keyContrast: Both land messianic fulfillment at the cross without inventing an Arminian/Reformed split on the vinegar.

verses.text: Let their table before them become a snare. May it become a retribution and a trap.
verses.arminianNotes:
Table become snare and trap. Wesley: punishment answers the sin of gall.

Imprecation is serious judicial plea, not private spite.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: Spirit-guided imprecation within duty; not reckless revenge. Table/snare seriousness.
verses.keyContrast: Both take imprecation seriously. Arminian readers find a judicial cry under oppression; Reformed interpreters emphasize Spirit-kept bounds and judgment on the reprobate.

verses.text: Let their eyes be darkened, so that they can’t see. Let their backs be continually bent.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eyes darkened; loins tremble. Wesley: minds judicially blinded; strength taken.

Judicial hardening warns against shutting eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: deprive of counsel and strength. Darkening.

verses.text: Pour out your indignation on them. Let the fierceness of your anger overtake them.
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks God to pour out his indignation and burning anger.

Both refuse to soft-pedal divine anger against persecutors of the godly.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: imprecations to terrify frantic enemies and comfort believers. Pour out.

verses.text: Let their habitation be desolate. Let no one dwell in their tents.
verses.arminianNotes:
He prays that their camp would be left desolate and their tents empty. Related judgment language appears in Acts 1:20.

Desolation of the hostile camp is prayed as public justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: wrath may reach posterity per the law’s threat. Either reading: desolate habitation.

verses.text: For they persecute him whom you have wounded. They tell of the sorrow of those whom you have hurt.
verses.arminianNotes:
Persecute whom you struck; recount the wounded’s pain. Wesley: barbarous cruelty; triumph in calamities.

Piling on the God-struck is extra guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: smitten as God’s child under discipline; persecuting the wounded adds damnation. Both sides agree: cruelty aggravates.

verses.text: Charge them with crime upon crime. Don’t let them come into your righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Punishment upon punishment; no acquittal. Wesley: give up to lusts; not partake mercy.

Exclusion from mercy is a sentence prayed against hardened foes.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: give over to reprobate mind; not enter righteousness. Both traditions see: no acquittal.

verses.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of life, and not be written with the righteous.
verses.arminianNotes:
Blotted from book of living; not enrolled with righteous. Wesley: eternal life.

Enrollment language warns—apostasy is not a game.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: book of life as election purpose; hypocrites blotted as openly rejected; elect finally not cut off. Shared seriousness; classic fork on perseverance.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat blotting as ultimate. Arminians typically hear exclusion from life; Reformed commentators often hear judgment revealing who were never written among the righteous.

verses.text: But I am in pain and distress. Let your salvation, God, protect me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Afflicted and in pain; salvation set me on high. Wesley: out of enemies’ reach.

Salvation lifts the poor sufferer who still asks.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: broken humility vs raging revenge; salvation shall exalt. Set on high.

verses.text: I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving.
verses.arminianNotes:
Praise with song; magnify with thanksgiving.

Both: praise is the fitting answer when God saves.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: elevated with joy; God magnified among men by praise. Song.

verses.text: It will please the LORD better than an ox, or a bull that has horns and hoofs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Pleases more than ox or bull. Wesley: hearty praise over glorious legal sacrifices.

Thanksgiving is the sacrifice God prefers—offer it.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: spiritual service preferred to Levitical pomp. Better than bull.

verses.text: The humble have seen it, and are glad. You who seek after God, let your heart live.
verses.arminianNotes:
Humble glad; seekers’ hearts revive. Wesley: dejected revived.

One deliverance revives many seekers.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: effects extend to others; pledge of grace. Both note: hearts revive.

verses.text: For the LORD hears the needy, and doesn’t despise his captive people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lord hears needy; does not despise prisoner-people. Wesley: prison or affliction for his sake.

Needy prayer is heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: deliverance of one signals care for all oppressed. Hears the needy.

verses.text: Let heaven and earth praise him; the seas, and everything that moves therein!
verses.arminianNotes:
Heaven, earth, seas praise.

Both widen praise beyond the individual.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: hyperbole teaching ardor; concern for Church preservation. All creation praise.

verses.text: For God will save Zion, and build the cities of Judah. They shall settle there, and own it.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will save Zion; build Judah; dwell and possess. Wesley: church and people; literal then heavenly Canaan.

Zion’s future is promised and believed.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: speaks for the Church; blessing from the sanctuary. Save Zion.

verses.text: The children also of his servants shall inherit it. Those who love his name shall dwell therein.
verses.arminianNotes:
Offspring of servants inherit; those who love his name dwell.

Loving the name is the mark of dwellers—love grace enables and requires.
verses.reformedNotes: Calvin: true seed who love the name, not hypocrite boasters. Love his name.
verses.keyContrast: Both end on lovers of the Name inheriting. Arminians stress love as living response; Reformed readers underline the true seed vs hypocrites.
